senses.def: to not have information about
to refuse to think about or pay attention to
to not understand, with the implication of a lack of capacity or ability
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἀθετέω ‘to set aside,’ not occurring in the NT) to believe that something or someone cannot be trusted or relied on and hence to reject
to refuse to recognize the validity of something
senses.comment: In Hebrews 10:28 the rejection may express itself in disobedience.

senses.def: pertaining to not ceasing from some activity

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a person not belonging to the ethnic group in question (from the specifically Jewish point of view, one who is not a Jew, but a Gentile)
to move up
senses.comment: The upward movement may be of almost any gradient, for example, in going up a road to Jerusalem (Galatians 1:17) or in going up into a tree (Luke 19:4) or in ascending into heaven (Acts 2:34).

senses.def: to move up onto an object, with specialization of meaning in reference to boats
to grow, as of plants, from the time of sprouting to mature size
to grow taller (restricted in the NT to the growth of plants)
(an idiom, literally: to arise in the heart) to begin to think about something
glosses: to have a thought occur to someone

senses.def: pertaining to what cannot be spoken against or objected to

senses.subdomain: Kinship Relations of the Same Generation
senses.def: the child of one’s uncle and aunt, either on the fathers side or the mothers side
senses.comment: Some languages make a clear distinction between so-called ‘parallel cousins’ and ‘cross cousins.’ Parallel cousins would be the offspring of one’s father’s brother or of one’s mother’s sister, while cross cousins would be the offspring of one’s father’s sister or of one’s mother’s brother. There is no way of knowing from the context of Colossians 4:10 what the specific relationship is between Mark and Barnabas, but for languages which have no general term for cousins, but only specific terms for parallel cousins or cross cousins, it is necessary to select one or another of these specific terms in speaking of Mark. By means of a footnote one can indicate that the Greek text does not specify which type of cousin is involved.

senses.def: to oppose someone, involving not only a psychological attitude but also a corresponding behavior
senses.comment: It may be that in some languages one can best render ἀντιτάσσομαι in Acts 18:6 as ‘to speak against,’ though in some languages opposition is often expressed idiomatically as ‘to show a sour face toward,’ ‘to have a mean heart toward,’ or ‘to turn one’s back on.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: uncircumcised in heart and ears) pertaining to being obdurate and obstinate
senses.comment: In the contexts illustrated by σκληροτράχηλος, ἀπερίτμητος καρδίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ὠσίν, and σκληροκαρδία, the focus of the stubbornness and obstinacy is the unwillingness to be taught or to understand.

senses.def: to wipe off, as a means of getting rid of some adhering substance
senses.comment: Since the action of wiping off the dust from one’s feet was a symbolic act of denunciation, it may be necessary in some languages to translate this expression in Luke 10:11 as ‘we wipe off as a way of denouncing you’ or ‘we wipe off as a way of showing how bad you are.’

senses.def: (derivative of ἄργυρος[a] ‘silver,’ 2.51) pertaining to being made or consisting of silver
an aromatic resin of a lily-like plant, often used for embalming a corpse
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ἄρωμα is ‘sweet-smelling herbs’ or ‘good-smelling leaves’ or ‘perfumed oil.’

senses.def: a hot steamy vapor
senses.comment: An important connotation in the use of the term ἀτμίς is the fact that it disappears so readily. This is a particularly significant element in James 4:14. The closest equivalent of ἀτμίς is normally a term which refers to the steam rising from a boiling pot or cauldron.

senses.def: pertaining to a complete lack of thankfulness
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀχάριστος in Luke 6:35, see ἀχάριστος[b] 33.353.

senses.def: pertaining to not being thankful
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀχάριστος in Luke 6:35, see ἀχάριστος[a] 25.101.

senses.def: (derivative of βέβαιος[b] ‘dependable, reliable,’ 31.90) to cause someone to be firm or established in belief
senses.comment: For another interpretation of βεβαιόω in Mark 16:20, see βεβαιόω[b] 28.44.

senses.def: to cause something to be known as certain
glosses: to prove to be true and certain
senses.comment: For another interpretation of βεβαιόω in Mark 16:20, see βεβαιόω[a] 31.91.

senses.def: to increase in inner strength, with the implication of greater firmness of character or attitude
glosses: to be strengthened in one’s heart

senses.def: to use a rope with a lead weight attached to it in order to measure the depth of water

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the inward parts of the body, either the digestive system (as in γαστέρες ἀργαί, literally ‘lazy bellies,’ but meaning ‘gluttons’ Titus 1:12) or the womb (in set phrases such as συλλαμβάνω ἐν γαστρί ‘to conceive’ Luke 1:31; ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχω ‘be pregnant’ Matthew 1:18 and elsewhere)
(a figurative extension of meaning of γαστήρ[a] ‘belly,’ 8.68) a person who habitually eats excessively
senses.comment: A glutton is often spoken of idiomatically, for example, ‘a large belly’ or ‘a person who is only a stomach’ or ‘a professional eater.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to have in the womb) to be in a state of pregnancy
senses.comment: This expression contrasts with the meaning of συλλαμβάνω[b], 23.49, in that it seems to focus more upon the state of pregnancy rather than the event of conception.|It is impossible to determine whether in Matthew 1:23 (ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται υἱόν ‘she will be pregnant and bear a son’) the focus is upon the state of pregnancy or the fact of conception (see 23.49).

senses.def: to make the marks that form words on a surface (paper or other material), using a marking instrument (such as a pen)
senses.comment: Since the knowledge of writing is almost universal, there is usually no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for writing. In some instances in which languages are only now being reduced to writing, a phrase is often employed, for example, ‘to make marks on paper’ or ‘to talk with lines’ or ‘to speak with paper.’

senses.def: (pass. form of the verb) what is written, referring to Scripture
exact meaning unsure; a soldier other than heavily armed infantry or horsemen
to give a judicial hearing in a legal matter
glosses: to hear a case in court
senses.comment: In some languages the most satisfactory way of speaking about ‘a court hearing’ is to describe the relationship between the principal participants. This may sometimes be done by translating ‘for a judge to listen to an accuser and a defender.’

senses.def: to make fun of someone by joking or jesting
(derivative of διώκω[c] ‘to persecute,’ 39.45) a person who engages in persecuting others

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: an exclamatory particle indicating surprise, indignation, or anger
senses.comment: If another language does not have a fully satisfactory particle expressing surprise, indignation, or anger, it is probably best to leave this particle untranslated, as, for example, in a number of translations into English which make no attempt to introduce a corresponding emotive particle.

senses.def: an object (not necessarily three-dimensional) which has been formed to resemble a person, god, animal, etc.
senses.comment: In certain contexts the referents of εἰκών[a], τύπος[b], and χάραγμα[b] may have special religious significance in that they may refer to idols, but the focal component for the translator is that of a likeness or resemblance (see 58.35). In contexts such as Matthew 22:20 an equivalent translation may be simply ‘a picture,’ but in Romans 1:23 and Acts 7:43 one may use the same expression as is employed to render εἴδωλον[a] ‘idol’ (6.97).

senses.subdomain: Same or Equivalent Kind or Class
senses.def: that which has the same form as something else
senses.comment: Since the expressions τοῦ χοϊκοῦ and τοῦ ἐπουρανίου refer to individuals, it is much more satisfactory to translate 1 Corinthians 15:49 as ‘just as we have the likeness of the man made of earth, so we will have the likeness of the Man from heaven.’|In 1 Corinthians 15:49 εἰκών designates similarity in class or kind, while in Romans 1:23 εἰκών indicates a fashioned object (see 6.96).

senses.subdomain: Pattern, Model, Example, and Corresponding Representation
senses.def: that which represents something else in terms of basic form and features
to pierce with a pointed instrument
oil extracted from the fruit of olive trees, used as food, medicine, for burning in lamps, and as perfume when mixed with sweet-smelling substances
senses.comment: See discussion of translational problems in 6.197.

senses.def: to make fun of someone by pretending that he is not what he is or by imitating him in a distorted manner
the content of thinking and reasoning
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to find noun-like words for thinking or reasoning and therefore it may be necessary to use a verb equivalent throughout. For example, in Luke 11:17 one may translate as ‘but Jesus knew what they were thinking.’

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of ἐξέλκω ‘to pull, to draw out,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause a change of belief so as to correspond more with the beliefs of the person or factor causing the change

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: to cause foam to occur on the surface of a liquid
senses.comment: ἐπαφρίζω occurs in the NT only in Jude 1:13 in a figurative context. It probably differs from ἀφρίζω (14.28) in emphasizing the greater degree or extent of foam on the surface.|In some languages the type of foam which would be referred to in Jude 1:13 is called ‘the saliva of the waves’ or ‘the whiteness of the waves.’ Since foaming at the mouth is also regarded as a sign of anger, it is possible to speak in some languages of the foam of the waves as being ‘the anger of the waves.’ In other languages one may speak simply of ‘the whiteness of the waves.’

senses.subdomain: Processes Involving the Mouth, Other Than Eating and Drinking
senses.def: to lick an object with the tongue
senses.comment: It may be necessary in some languages to be somewhat more specific in the expression ‘licked his sores’ so that the text may read ‘licked the pus from his sores.’

senses.def: appearing to someone or at some place
pertaining to that which is different in kind or class from all other entities
pertaining to being broad and spacious, with the implication of agreeable and pleasant
expressing of forceful differences of opinion without necessarily having a presumed goal of seeking a solution
(derivative of θάμβος ‘astonishment,’ 25.208) to experience astonishment as the result of some unusual event
pertaining to being liable to death (that which will eventually die)
senses.comment: The phrase ‘mortal bodies’ (Romans 6:12) may be rendered as ‘bodies which will die.’

senses.def: the city of Jerusalem, including its inhabitants
the heavenly Jerusalem of the future
Italy

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: points of time consisting of occasions for particular events
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no general term for ‘time’ or ‘occasion.’ In some contexts it is simply not necessary to have such a term. For example, in rendering Matthew 13:30 one may translate ‘when the harvest comes, I will say to the reapers’ or ‘when people begin to harvest, I will say to the reapers.’ In other contexts, a term which normally refers to some unit is employed in a generic sense, as in the case of Greek ὥρα which means literally ‘hour’ but is frequently used as a generic expression for a point of time, as in Matthew 8:13. In Acts 7:17 χρόνος may often be rendered by a generic expression such as ‘day,’ for example, ‘when it was almost the day for God to keep his promise.’ In the case of Matthew 26:45, the nearness of the time may be indicated as ‘very soon the Son of Man will be handed over.’|Though it seems quite ordinary in English for one to speak of ‘time coming’ or ‘… drawing near,’ this type of figurative usage is impossible in many languages. The equivalent may be simply ‘will soon be’ or ‘is about to happen.’ The expression οὔπω ἥκει ἡ ὥρα μου (literally ‘my time has not yet come’) in John 2:4 denotes that it is not yet the occasion for a particular event (see καιρός in John 7:8 and compare John 7:10) but that it will soon be. In these contexts the expression may be rendered as ‘there is still time’ or ‘I will soon do it.’ In John 7:30 and John 8:20 (οὔπω ἐληλύθει ἡ ὥρα αὐτοῦ ‘his time has not yet come’) the reference is to the occasion of his eventual arrest, implying that it will indeed happen.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: an indefinite unit of time (the actual extent of time being determined by the context)

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: an indefinite period of time, but probably with the implication of the relation of a period to a particular state of affairs
a favorable opportunity or occasion in view of propitious circumstances
senses.comment: It is possible to interpret καιρός in Acts 24:25 merely as an ‘occasion’ (see 67.1). In fact, one may translate simply as ‘and when I have time, I will call you.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a relatively short period of time, with emphasis upon the temporary nature of the event or state

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a relatively short period of time, with emphasis upon the temporary nature of the event or state

senses.subdomain: To Distinguish, To Evaluate, To Judge
senses.def: to judge as a referee that someone is not worthy to receive a prize
glosses: to judge as not worthy of a reward

senses.def: to be completely capable of doing or experiencing something
senses.comment: For another interpretation of κατισχύω in Luke 21:36, see 79.64.

senses.def: to be physically strong enough for some purpose
senses.comment: For another interpretation of κατισχύω in Luke 21:36, see 74.10.

senses.def: to prevail over something or some person so as to be able to defeat, with the implication that the successful participant has greater strength
senses.comment: In some languages it may be impossible to personify ‘death’ and thus make it an agent of ‘defeating.’ However, it is possible to retain some of the figurative meaning involved, at least in some languages, by translating ‘and my church will never die out’ or ‘and my church will never die.’

senses.def: (derivative of κιθάρα lyre, harp, 6.83) to play a lyre, a small stringed harp-like instrument held in the hands and plucked
to punish, with the implication of resulting severe suffering
senses.comment: In a number of languages punishment is often expressed as a causative of suffering, that is to say, ‘to cause to suffer’ or ‘to cause to endure harm.’ In some languages, however, there are a number of different types of punishment, and clear distinctions must be made between various degrees of punishment as well as between physical versus mental punishment.

senses.def: a grain somewhat similar to wheat, but regarded as less desirable for food
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no specific term for barley, and therefore it may be useful simply to borrow a term from a dominant language. In certain instances, however, translators have used an expression such as ‘wheat-like grain.’ It may even be useful to have a footnote to explain something of the nature of barley, but the fact that it was cheaper than wheat is clear from Revelation 6:6.

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: pertaining to not being able to be known by the public but known by some in-group or by those immediately involved
an area in Jerusalem, paved with flat blocks of stone and forming a kind of courtyard (not a thoroughfare)
senses.comment: In some languages one may describe ‘The Stone Pavement’ as ‘a court covered with large blocks of flat stone’ or ‘a stone-paved courtyard.’ See 93.437.

senses.def: a region in the Sinai peninsula and nearby Arabia
serious conflict, either physical or non-physical, but clearly intensive and bitter
senses.comment: In order to suggest something of the intensity of conflict in μάχομαι and μάχη, it may be useful in some instances to employ similes in the rendering of these terms, for example, ‘they opposed one another just as though they were actually fighting one another’ or ‘they are fighting, as it were.’

senses.def: to cause a state to cease, with the implication of force
(derivative of μισθόομαι ‘to hire,’ 57.172) a person who has been hired to perform a particular service or work
the leader of the Israelites out of Egypt and the lawgiver
the Law given through Moses, as formulated in the first five books of the OT
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is quite appropriate to refer to the writings of a person by simply mentioning the author, but in many languages this cannot be done. Furthermore, in 2 Corinthians 3:15 it may be necessary to employ an active expression, so that one must translate ‘whenever people read the laws which God gave through Moses.’ The use of Μωϋσῆς as a reference to the Law of Moses also occurs in the phrase ‘Moses and the prophets’ as a reference to the sacred writings (compare ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται ‘the sacred writings,’ 33.58).

senses.def: to comprehend something on the basis of careful thought and consideration
to think over a matter with care

senses.subdomain: Have an Opinion, Hold a View
senses.def: to be able to form some idea about
glosses: to be able to form an idea
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand νοέω in Ephesians 3:20 as meaning merely ‘to hold a particular view’ (compare 31.1), and therefore one may translate ‘far beyond what we think to be the case.’

senses.def: a Hebrew king in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:8)
pertaining to having the same kinds of feelings or desires

to affirm the truth of a statement by calling on a divine being to execute sanctions against a person if the statement in question is not true (in the case of a deity taking an oath, his divine being is regarded as validating the statement)
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific in referring to the swearing of an oath, for example, ‘to say something by calling upon God to listen’ or ‘to state that something is true and asking God to punish if it is not true’ or ‘to make God responsible for what one has said.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a casual non-membership group of people, fairly large in size and assembled for whatever purpose
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no term corresponding to ‘crowd.’ One may, however, usually speak of such a group of people as ‘many people’ or ‘many men and women.’ Depending on the context, it may besary to indicate some relative difference in size, for example, ‘very large crowd’ or ‘many, many people.’ If the crowd is relatively small, one may sometimes speak of ‘just some people.’

senses.subdomain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
senses.def: the common people, in contrast with those who are rich, leaders, and/or authorities in the society, often with the implication of disdain and low esteem
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘the common people’ is ‘the poor people,’ but in some languages an equivalent depends upon geographical location, for example, ‘those who live on the edge of town’ (the opposite situation from what exists in most present-day metropolitan centers). In still other languages ‘the common people’ may be designated in terms of lack of status, for example, ‘those who have no position’ or ‘those whom the rich do not greet’ or ‘those before whom no one ever bows.’

senses.def: pertaining to being difficult to be believed
senses.comment: It would also be possible to translate εἴδομεν παράδοξα σήμερον as ‘we have seen today things we can hardly believe’ or even ‘… things which people would scarcely believe.’ For another interpretation of παράδοξος in Luke 5:26, see 58.56.

senses.def: pertaining to that which is unusual in the sense of contrary to expectations
senses.comment: For another interpretation of παράδοξος in Luke 5:26, see 31.44.

senses.def: to place something around an object or area
act of trying to learn the nature or character of someone or something by submitting such to thorough and extensive testing
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand πειράζω and ἐκπειράζω in Matthew 16:1 and Luke 10:25 as meaning ‘to try to trap’ (see 27.31). See also 88.308.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: act of endeavoring or attempting to cause someone to sin
to tear off or to strip off, as of clothing
to fashion or form an object
to give a particular form to something
a quantity many times greater than normally expected

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to the older of two objects

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: pertaining to a person who has lived in ancient times, that is to say, at a point long before the point of time of the discourse itself (πρεσβύτερος[b] may also carry the implication of prestige)
an adult male or female advanced in years
a person of responsibility and authority in matters of socio-religious concerns, both in Jewish and Christian societies
senses.comment: In some languages πρεσβύτερος[b] is best rendered as ‘older leaders,’ but in other languages the more appropriate term would be the equivalent of ‘counselor,’ since it would be assumed that counselors would be older than the average person in a group as well as having authority to lead and direct activities.

senses.def: a person several preceding generations removed from the reference person
senses.comment: In a number of languages one’s forefathers may be referred to simply as ‘fathers who have long since died.’ In other languages they may be referred to as ‘fathers of other generations’ or ‘fathers of ancient times.’

senses.def: to add something to an existing quantity
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is not at all difficult to speak of ‘adding things,’ but to add events may provide some special difficulties in restructuring. For example, in Luke 3:20 it may be important to translate as ‘he had done many other bad things, but he also did this,’ and in Galatians 2:6 it may be helpful to translate ‘for those who were of repute did not say that I should do anything more than I was doing.’

senses.def: to place something at the disposal of someone else
(a Semitic idiom, literally: to place with his fathers) to carry out a burial procedure
to continue, with focus upon the next element
to mark an immediately following event
(derivative of ῥοῖζος ‘the noise made by something passing swiftly through the air,’ not occurring in the NT) pertaining to a sudden noise made by swift movement
senses.comment: The expression ‘with a rushing noise’ may be rendered as ‘suddenly and with a roar’ or ‘quickly and with a lot of noise.’

senses.def: the plain along the coast of Palestine
to do something hurriedly, with the implication of associated energy
senses.comment: For another interpretation of σπεύδω in Acts 20:16, see 25.74.

senses.def: to cause something to happen soon
senses.comment: It is also possible to render this meaning of σπεύδω in 2 Peter 3:12 as ‘doing your best to cause …’

senses.subdomain: Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
senses.def: to be eager to do something, with the implication of readiness to expend energy and effort
senses.comment: For another interpretation of σπεύδω in Acts 20:16, see 68.79.

senses.def: the chief legal official of a city
senses.comment: In a number of instances στρατηγός may be rendered simply as ‘the chief of the town’ or ‘the ruler of the city.’

senses.def: (a title, literally: official of the temple) a commander of Jewish soldiers responsible for guarding and maintaining order in the Jewish Temple
to feel sorrow or grief together with someone or at the same time
to be destroyed together with someone or something else
senses.comment: In a number of languages one must translate συναπόλλυμαι in Hebrews 11:31 as ‘to die,’ for example, ‘Rahab the harlot did not die with those who were disobedient.’

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: a plan for taking secret action against someone or some institution, with the implication of an oath binding the conspirators
a room in the interior of a house, normally without windows opening to the outside
senses.comment: In Luke 12:3 the emphasis is upon the strictly private location of the inner room. In such a context one may translate ‘a strictly private room’ or ‘a small room in the center of the house.’

senses.def: a room for the storage of valuables
senses.comment: ταμεῖον[b] and θησαυρός[a] may often be rendered by descriptive phrases, for example, ‘a room where valuable things are kept’ or ‘a place where valuables are stored.’|In Matthew 12:35 θησαυρός[a] is used figuratively (ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ ἐκβάλλει ἀγαθά ‘a good man draws good things from his good storehouse,’ meaning ‘… storehouse of good things’) to describe the heart as a kind of storehouse or treasure.

senses.def: one who customarily engages in a particular craft or occupation
cardinal number, where there are three thousand instances of a countable entity
to obey on the basis of having paid attention to
senses.comment: Terms expressing the concept of ‘obedience’ may frequently be rendered in some languages as ‘to do what one says’ or ‘to carry out someone’s orders.’

senses.def: to respond to someone knocking or calling at a door
to cause to recall and to think about again
glosses: to cause to think about again
senses.comment: In 2 Timothy 1:5 the phrase ὑπόμνησιν λαμβάνω may be interpreted as a causative passive phrase (compare λαμβάνω in 90.63 and 90.85), for example, ὑπόμνησιν λαβὼν τῆς ἐν σοὶ ἀνυποκρίτου πίστεως ‘I have been reminded of your sincere faith,’ but it may also be appropriately rendered as an instance of active remembering and accordingly translated as ‘I remember the sincere faith that you have.’|It is also possible to interpret ὑπόμνησις in 2 Peter 1:13 as meaning simply ‘to remember,’ and therefore one may translate as ‘to stir you up as you remember.’

senses.def: a procurator of Palestine
to put on and to wear clothes
to be in a particular state or condition
(an idiom, literally: to bear the sword) to have the capacity or authority to punish
glosses: to have the power to punish

senses.def: (derivative of χαλκός[a] ‘bronze, brass, copper,’ 2.54) pertaining to being made or consisting of bronze, brass, or copper
eloquent and attractive speech involving pleasing rhetorical devices
to acquire possessions or services in exchange for money
